procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated August 26, 1955, of the Election Tribunal, Patiala, in Election Petition No. 12 of 1954, declaring the two appellants' election to be void.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appeal by special leave is directed against the majority judgment and order of the Election Tribunal of Patiala.

directions: The appeal is dismissed with costs to the con-testing respondents.

issue.issue_text: Whether the rejection of the nomination paper of the 18th respondent by the Returning Officer was justified on the grounds that the thumb impressions of the proposer and seconder had not been properly verified according to the Election Rules.

facts: The nomination paper of the 18th respondent was rejected by the Returning Officer.
The reason for rejection was that the thumb impressions of the proposer and seconder were allegedly not attested in accordance with Election Rules.
The thumb impressions had been attested by a local magistrate.
The Election Tribunal found as a matter of fact that this specific magistrate had been authorized by the Election Commission for this purpose.
However, there was a clerical error or a "mistake of omission" in the official communication from the Election Commission to the local election officer about the magistrate's authorization.
law: The relevant Election Rule states that a person unable to write their name can sign by placing a mark (like a thumb impression) on a paper in the presence of an officer specified by the Election Commission.
This specified officer must be satisfied as to the person's identity and then attest the mark.
application: The Supreme Court treated the issue as "essentially one of fact."

The Court accepted the Tribunal's factual finding that the magistrate who attested the thumb impressions had indeed been authorized by the Election Commission, despite the clerical error in the communication.
The Court held that this clerical error did not invalidate the attestation, as the underlying fact was that the magistrate was authorized.
The Court refused to accept the argument that a clerical or accidental mistake could render an otherwise valid attestation unacceptable in principle.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because the thumb impressions were attested by a magistrate who was, in fact, authorized by the Election Commission, the attestation was valid. Therefore, the Returning Officer was not justified in rejecting the nomination paper on this ground.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Election Tribunal was wrong in holding that there is a presumption that the improper rejection of a nomination paper materially affected the result of the election.

law.fact: The Supreme Court affirmed the legal principle that in cases of improper rejection of a nomination paper, there is a presumption that the result of the election has been materially affected.
law.relevant_text: So far as the latter class of cases is concerned, it may be pointed out that almost all the Election Tribunals in t11e country have consistently taken the view that there is a presumption in the case of improper rejection of a nomination paper that it has materially affected the result of the election.

law.fact: The Court distinguished between the legal effect of an 'improper rejection' and an 'improper acceptance' of a nomination paper, noting that the presumption applies to the former but not necessarily the latter.
law.relevant_text: It appears that though the words of the section are in general terms with equal application to the case of improper acceptance, as also of improper rejection of a nomination paper, case law has made a distinction between the two classes of cases.

application.fact: The Court acknowledged the appellant's argument that the statute requires the petitioner to prove that the improper rejection 'materially affected' the result. However, it found that this burden is discharged by the legal presumption that arises in such cases.
application.relevant_text: The contention further is that ss. 101 and 102. oi the Evidence Act must therefore apply and the burden must be cast on the petitioner before the Tribunal to establish both the conditions before any relief could be granted to him. In our opinion, that argument does not advance the case of the appellants any more than what has been laid down by this Court in the cases referred to above. The other provisions of the Evidence Act including the rules of presumption must also be equally applicable.

application.fact: The Court justified this presumption on practical grounds, stating it is nearly impossible for a petitioner to prove how electors would have voted if the rejected candidate had been on the ballot. The very act of excluding a candidate from the election is considered a material factor in itself.
application.relevant_text: Apart from the practical difficulty, almost the impossibility, of demonstrating that the electors would have cast their votes in a particular way... the fact that one of several candidates for an elecion had been kept out of the arena is by itself a very material consideration.

application.fact: The Court noted that this long-standing judicial view was later given 'legislative sanction' through an amendment to the election law, which made improper rejection conclusive proof that an election is void. This reinforced the correctness of the presumption.
application.relevant_text: The conjecture therefore is permissible that the legislature realising the difference between the two classes of cases has given legislative sanction to the view by amending •· 100 by the Representation of the People (Second Amendment) Act, XXVII of 1956, and by going to the length of providing that an improper rejection of any nomination paper is conclusive proof of the election being void.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument and held that the Election Tribunal was correct. The Court affirmed that there is a legal presumption that the improper rejection of a nomination paper materially affects the result of an election. This presumption is based on the practical impossibility of proving how votes would have been cast and the inherent material impact of excluding a candidate from the contest. Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in its finding.

issue.issue_text: Whether the election of the second appellant in respect of the reserved seat should not have been set aside, even if the election was declared void as a whole.

facts: The case involved an election for a double-seat constituency, which the Court considered to be 'one integral whole'.
The Election Tribunal found that a nomination paper had been improperly rejected, which materially affected the result of the election.
The appellants argued that even if the election was void, the result for the second appellant in the reserved seat should be allowed to stand.
law: Section 100 of the governing Act states that if an Election Tribunal finds that the result of an election has been materially affected by the improper rejection of a nomination paper, the Tribunal 'shall declare the election to be wholly void'.
application: The Court emphasized that the language of Section 100 is mandatory ('shall declare').
Because the election for the double-seat constituency was a single, integrated event, the finding that it was materially affected by the improper rejection required the entire election to be voided.

The Court reasoned that if the election had to be declared void, it must be declared void 'as a whole,' leaving no room to save the result of one part of it (the reserved seat) while nullifying the other.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that because the election for the double-seat constituency was a single, integral event and Section 100 of the Act mandates that such an election be declared 'wholly void' due to the improper rejection of a nomination, the Tribunal was justified in setting aside the election as a whole, including the result for the reserved seat.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the rejection of the nomination paper of the 18th respondent by the Returning Officer was justified on the grounds that the thumb impressions of the proposer and seconder had not been properly verified according to the Election Rules.
appellant_arguments: A mistake of omission in the communication from the Election Commission to the local election officer, even if clerical or accidental, rendered the attestation of the thumb impressions by the magistrate unacceptable and invalid.
Therefore, the Returning Officer was justified in rejecting the nomination paper.
respondent_arguments: The persons whose thumb impressions were on the nomination paper had genuinely proposed and seconded the candidate.
The magistrate who attested the thumb impressions had, as a matter of fact, been authorized by the Election Commission to do so, regardless of any clerical error in communication.
Therefore, the attestation was valid, and the rejection of the nomination paper was improper.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Election Tribunal was wrong in holding that there is a presumption that the improper rejection of a nomination paper materially affected the result of the election.
appellant_arguments: Section 100(1)(c) of the Act places 'improper acceptance' and 'improper rejection' of a nomination on the same footing.
The law requires two cumulative conditions to be met to void an election: (1) an improper rejection and (2) that the rejection materially affected the result.

Based on Supreme Court precedents (Vashisht Narain Sharma v. Dev Chandra and Hari Vishnu Karnath v. Syed Ahmad lshaque) and the Evidence Act, the burden of establishing both conditions lies on the petitioner who seeks to have the election set aside.
There should be no automatic presumption that an improper rejection materially affected the result.
respondent_arguments: In cases of improper rejection of a nomination paper, there is a strong presumption that the result of the election has been materially affected.
This view is consistently held by Election Tribunals across the country.
The burden lies on the person seeking to uphold the election (the appellant) to rebut this presumption.
It is practically impossible for a petitioner to demonstrate how electors would have voted if the rejected candidate had been in the contest.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the election of the second appellant in respect of the reserved seat should not have been set aside, even if the election was declared void as a whole.
appellant_arguments: The election for the reserved seat should have been treated separately and not set aside along with the general election.
respondent_arguments: The election was for a double-seat constituency and was a single, integral event.
Under Section 100, if the result is found to be materially affected by an improper rejection, the Tribunal must declare the election 'wholly void'.
Therefore, the Tribunal was correct to set aside the election as a whole, including the result for the reserved seat.

cases.case_name: Chatturbhuj Vithaldas Jasani v. Moreshwar Parashram
cases.principle: The improper rejection of a nomination paper 'affects the whole election'.

cases.case_name: Karnail Singh v. Election Tribunal, Hissar
cases.principle: For the similar view that the improper rejection of a nomination paper affects the whole election.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In a case where a nomination paper has been improperly rejected, there is a strong presumption that the result of the election has been materially affected, and the burden of proof lies on the person seeking to uphold the election to rebut that presumption.
obiter: While the words of the statute place improper acceptance and improper rejection of a nomination on the same footing, case law has distinguished between the two classes of cases.
It is practically difficult, almost impossible, to demonstrate that electors would have cast their votes in a particular way for a rejected candidate.
The fact that one of several candidates for an election has been kept out of the arena is by itself a very material consideration.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In cases of improper rejection of a nomination paper, there is a strong presumption that the result of the election has been materially affected. This presumption arises from the practical impossibility of proving how electors would have voted for a candidate who was kept out of the contest, and the fact that excluding a candidate is itself a very material consideration. This distinguishes improper rejection from improper acceptance, where proof of the effect on the result may be more easily demonstrated.
legal_tests_applied: Section 100(1)(c) of the Representation of the People Act: An election shall be declared wholly void if the Tribunal is of the opinion that the result of the election has been materially affected by the improper acceptance or rejection of any nomination.

Presumption of Material Effect: In cases of improper rejection of a nomination paper, there is a presumption that the result of the election has been materially affected, and the burden lies on the person seeking to uphold the election to rebut this presumption.
why_appellant_lost: The court deferred to the Election Tribunal's finding of fact that the magistrate who attested the thumb impressions had, in fact, been authorized by the Election Commission, making a clerical error in communication insufficient to invalidate the nomination.

The court rejected the argument that improper acceptance and improper rejection of a nomination must be treated identically under the statute, holding that case law has established a distinction between the two, with improper rejection giving rise to a presumption of material effect.

The court refused to re-examine the evidence intended to rebut the presumption, stating that as a court of special leave appeal, it "does not ordinarily reopen findings of fact recorded by a competent Tribunal."

The court held that under Section 100, once it is found that an improper rejection materially affected the result, the Tribunal is mandated to declare the election "wholly void," and since the election for a double-seat constituency was "one integral whole," the election for the reserved seat could not be saved.
why_respondent_won: The court upheld the Tribunal's finding that the nomination paper was improperly rejected because the attesting magistrate was, as a matter of fact, authorized to perform the attestation.
The court affirmed the long-standing view of Election Tribunals that there is a presumption that the improper rejection of a nomination paper materially affects the election result.
The court agreed that the burden of proof to rebut this presumption fell on the appellants, and the Tribunal was justified in finding they had not met that burden.

The court found that the plain language of Section 100 required the Tribunal to declare the election "wholly void" once the conditions were met, justifying the decision to set aside the election in its entirety for the double-seat constituency.
policy_considerations: The court acknowledged the "practical difficulty, almost the impossibility, of demonstrating that the electors would have cast their votes in a particular way" for a candidate who was improperly rejected.

The court reasoned that "the fact that one of several candidates for an elecion had been kept out of the arena is by itself a very material consideration," as it may have prevented electors from voting for the best or most formidable candidate available.

The court noted that a subsequent amendment to the Act, making improper rejection conclusive proof of a void election, provided "legislative sanction" to the judicial view that improper rejection is a more serious defect than improper acceptance.
